quiz.q: Sri Lanka's drug laws can impose the death penalty for trafficking above what quantity of heroin or cocaine?
quiz.explanation: Sri Lanka's Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance allows the death penalty for trafficking above 2 grams of heroin or cocaine — one of the lowest thresholds globally, making it possible to face execution for very small trafficking quantities.

laws.title: Section 365A Criminalizes Same-Sex Conduct
laws.subtitle: Sri Lanka retains British colonial-era law criminalizing 'gross indecency' between men
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka retains Sections 365 and 365A of its Penal Code, which criminalize 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' and 'gross indecency,' with penalties of up to 10 years imprisonment for men. Lesbianism is not explicitly criminalized but faces severe social stigma. LGBTQ+ Sri Lankans face significant discrimination in healthcare, employment, and housing. LGBTQ+ advocacy organizations exist but operate carefully. There have been parliamentary discussions about decriminalization, but no legislative change has occurred. The Colombo Pride Walk has been held in recent years.
laws.penalty: Same-sex conduct between men is punishable by up to 10 years imprisonment under Sections 365 and 365A
exceptions: Female same-sex conduct is not explicitly criminalized under current law

quiz.q: What is the maximum imprisonment penalty for male same-sex conduct under Sri Lanka's Penal Code?
quiz.explanation: Sri Lanka's Sections 365 and 365A of the Penal Code criminalize same-sex conduct between men with up to 10 years imprisonment, a law inherited from British colonial rule.

laws.title: Post-War Press Freedom Challenges
laws.subtitle: Sri Lanka's press freedom improved after the civil war era but challenges remain
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka's constitution protects freedom of expression and press. During the civil war (1983-2009) and its aftermath, journalists faced murder, disappearance, and exile — particularly those covering Tamil issues. Lasantha Wickrematunge, editor of the Sunday Leader, was murdered in 2009. Post-war, Sri Lanka has shown some improvement in press freedom. However, the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) has been used against journalists, and online publications face vague laws. The 2022 economic crisis and protests were covered relatively freely. Sri Lanka still ranks in the lower half globally for press freedom.
laws.penalty: Prevention of Terrorism Act can be applied to journalists; criminal defamation law exists; past journalist murders are largely unresolved
exceptions: Significant improvement since the civil war period

quiz.q: What was the fate of investigative journalist Lasantha Wickrematunge in Sri Lanka in 2009?
options: He was expelled from the country
He was sentenced to hard labor
quiz.explanation: Lasantha Wickrematunge, editor of the Sunday Leader newspaper and a prominent investigative journalist, was murdered in January 2009 — shortly after writing an editorial predicting his own assassination. His case remains emblematic of the dangers journalists faced in Sri Lanka during and after the civil war.

laws.title: Social Media Blocking During Crises and Personal Data Law
laws.subtitle: Sri Lanka has blocked social media during riots and is developing data protection legislation
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka has blocked social media platforms during civil unrest on multiple occasions. During the anti-Muslim riots in 2018, social media was blocked to prevent spread of hate content. During the 2022 economic crisis protests, social media access was briefly restricted. Sri Lanka's Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) was passed in 2022, establishing a data protection framework. The Telecommunications Regulatory Commission (TRC) has authority to block content. Sri Lanka's ICT Agency manages digital government services. Social media blocking has been controversial and subject to legal challenges.
laws.penalty: TRC authority to block platforms; PDPA: fines for data protection violations; blocking contested in courts
exceptions: Judicial challenges to blocking have had mixed results

quiz.q: During what Sri Lankan crisis in 2022 was social media access restricted?
options: The economic crisis and mass protests that forced President Rajapaksa to flee
quiz.explanation: During Sri Lanka's devastating 2022 economic crisis — when mass protests forced President Gotabaya Rajapaksa to flee — the government briefly restricted social media access, attempting to limit protest coordination, though the digital restrictions failed to stop the historic uprising.

laws.title: CBSL Banking Rules & Economic Crisis Debt Restructuring
laws.subtitle: Sri Lanka defaulted on foreign debt in 2022, requiring IMF rescue and banking sector reforms
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka's Central Bank (CBSL) regulates all licensed commercial banks, specialized banks, and finance companies. Sri Lanka experienced a catastrophic economic crisis in 2022 — it defaulted on its foreign debt (the first in its history), faced fuel shortages, and suffered 70%+ inflation. Months-long blackouts and medicine shortages led to mass protests that toppled the government. An IMF Extended Fund Facility program was agreed in 2023, requiring banking sector reforms, improved state bank governance, and fiscal consolidation. Sri Lanka's State Bank (Bank of Ceylon, People's Bank) dominance raised governance concerns. The CBSL issued guidelines on digital currency and has a cautious approach to crypto.
laws.penalty: Banking Act violations: fines up to LKR 5 million per offense; unlicensed financial services: imprisonment up to 5 years; IMF program conditionality violations: risk of program suspension and loss of disbursements
exceptions: State banks have government guarantee implicit exemptions from some market conduct rules
Specialized agricultural banks have modified capital requirements
Microfinance institutions have simplified licensing under Microfinance Act

quiz.q: What historic financial event did Sri Lanka experience in 2022 for the first time in its history?
options: Adoption of the US dollar as legal tender
Default on its foreign debt obligations
quiz.explanation: In April 2022, Sri Lanka made its first-ever default on foreign debt, unable to service approximately $51 billion in external obligations. The crisis stemmed from depleted foreign reserves, compounded by tax cuts, COVID tourism losses, and poor economic management.

laws.title: FSQD Food Safety & Sri Lankan Cinnamon and Tea Heritage
laws.subtitle: Sri Lanka's food safety authority protects its world-famous true cinnamon and Ceylon tea
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka's Food Safety and Quality Division (FSQD) under the Ministry of Health regulates food safety. Sri Lanka has globally significant agricultural heritage: Sri Lanka (formerly Ceylon) produces 'true cinnamon' (Cinnamomum verum) — also called Ceylon cinnamon — as opposed to cassia (Cinnamomum aromaticum, sometimes sold as 'cinnamon' elsewhere). Sri Lanka produces approximately 80-90% of the world's true cinnamon and has GI protection for it. Ceylon tea — grown in the hill country (Nuwara Eliya, Dimbula, Uva) — is another globally recognized product. Sri Lanka's Tea Board and Spices Authority manage export quality. The 2019 Easter Sunday bombings severely impacted tourism food service. Sri Lanka's economic crisis (2022) complicated food import and food safety oversight.
laws.penalty: FSQD violations: fines up to LKR 1 million; Ceylon cinnamon GI fraud: Sri Lanka Customs rejection; tea export quality failures: Tea Board de-certification; food safety failures at tourist premises: FSQD closure orders
exceptions: Small village spice producers selling to local collectors have simplified FSQD requirements
Traditional home cooking using own-grown vegetables and spices is unregulated
Subsistence fishing communities selling direct at beach markets have simplified MOH inspection
laws.sourceLabel: Sri Lanka Ministry of Health - Food Safety

quiz.q: What distinguishes 'true cinnamon' (Ceylon cinnamon) from cassia, and why does Sri Lanka's dominance matter?
options: True cinnamon is legally only from Sri Lanka — all other countries produce a different spice
Ceylon cinnamon (Cinnamomum verum) has thinner, softer quills and lower coumarin content than cassia — Sri Lanka produces 80-90% of the world's true cinnamon
True cinnamon must be organic certified — Sri Lanka was first country to achieve 100% organic cinnamon
Sri Lanka's cinnamon has UN protected status preventing any other country from using the cinnamon name
quiz.explanation: Ceylon cinnamon (Cinnamomum verum) has thin, papery quills, complex flavor, and crucially, much lower coumarin content than cassia (which can cause liver damage in high doses). Sri Lanka produces 80-90% of world true cinnamon supply. The EU actually limits cassia-derived 'cinnamon' in products for coumarin reasons — making genuine Ceylon cinnamon important for health reasons.

laws.title: Sri Lanka Animal Welfare Bill and Stray Dog Management
laws.subtitle: Sri Lanka passed landmark Animal Welfare Act in 2023
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka enacted a landmark Animal Welfare Act in 2023 after decades of advocacy — replacing the colonial-era Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Ordinance (No. 13 of 1907). The new Act significantly modernizes Sri Lankan animal welfare law, introducing criminal penalties for cruelty with imprisonment, establishing minimum care standards, and addressing companion animal welfare. Sri Lanka has a significant stray dog population and has adopted a national rabies control program using TNR and vaccination rather than mass culling — a policy supported by the WHO. The Act covers companion animals, working animals, and entertainment animals. Sri Lanka also has specific protections for elephants under the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance — the elephant is the national animal.
laws.penalty: Animal cruelty under new Act: up to 2 years imprisonment and fines; repeat offenders: increased penalties; ban on keeping animals in serious cases
exceptions: Livestock farming
Buddhist temple elephant practices
Licensed wildlife research
Traditional fishing

quiz.q: What approach has Sri Lanka adopted for stray dog management in its national rabies control program?
options: TNR (trap-neuter-return) and vaccination rather than mass culling — supported by the WHO
Dog meat legalization to reduce population
quiz.explanation: Sri Lanka adopted a TNR (trap-neuter-return) and vaccination approach to stray dog management in its national rabies control program — a method supported by the WHO as more effective and humane than mass culling for sustainable rabies control.

laws.title: Sri Lanka Personal Laws — General, Muslim, Kandyan, Tesawalamai
laws.subtitle: Sri Lanka has four different personal law systems
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka has four distinct personal law systems applying to different communities: the General Law (Marriage Registration Ordinance, Divorce Act — applying to most Sri Lankans); the Muslim Marriage and Divorce Act (MMDA, applying to Muslims); the Kandyan Marriage and Divorce Act (for Kandyan Sinhalese); and Tesawalamai (customary law applying to Jaffna Tamils). The MMDA has been criticized extensively — it sets no minimum age for Muslim marriages, does not require the bride's consent for her registration, and allows polygamy. Attempts to reform the MMDA have been blocked for decades despite significant advocacy. Sri Lanka does not recognize same-sex relationships. Domestic violence is addressed through the Prevention of Domestic Violence Act 2005.
laws.penalty: Civil and criminal enforcement varying by personal law system; MMDA violations: limited enforcement; domestic violence: protective orders and imprisonment
exceptions: Muslim personal law significantly different from General Law
Kandyan customary provisions for land inheritance
Tesawalamai customary property rights for Jaffna Tamils
laws.sourceLabel: Sri Lanka Marriage Registration Ordinance & MMDA

quiz.q: What significant reform gap exists in Sri Lanka's Muslim Marriage and Divorce Act (MMDA)?
options: The MMDA requires all marriages to be in Arabic
The MMDA sets no minimum age for Muslim marriages and does not require the bride's own consent for registration
The MMDA requires all Muslim marriages to be approved by the Supreme Court
quiz.explanation: Sri Lanka's Muslim Marriage and Divorce Act (MMDA) has been widely criticized for setting no minimum age for Muslim marriages and not requiring the bride's own consent for registration of the marriage. Reform attempts have been blocked for decades, leaving Muslim women and girls in Sri Lanka with significantly fewer protections than women under the General Law.

laws.title: Sri Lanka Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act
laws.subtitle: Foreign ownership limits and housing rights
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka restricts foreign land ownership under the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act (2014), which prohibits foreigners from owning land (purchases or leases over 1 year) except through companies with less than 50% foreign shareholding, or in designated export processing zones. Foreign nationals can own condominium units above the 4th floor. Long-term leases up to 99 years are permitted. The Rent Act (No. 7 of 1972) protects long-term tenants of older properties with controlled rents, though most properties entered unregulated market by the 2000s. Sri Lanka's 2022 economic crisis caused widespread mortgage defaults and housing instability.
laws.penalty: Illegal foreign land purchase: void and subject to forfeiture; Rent Act violation: Rent Board complaint available
exceptions: Foreign nationals restricted to condominium above 4th floor
2022 economic crisis caused widespread property market distress
laws.source: Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act 2014; Rent Act No. 7/1972
laws.sourceLabel: Sri Lanka Foreign Land Ownership Act

quiz.q: What floor restriction applies to foreign nationals wishing to own property in Sri Lanka?
quiz.explanation: Sri Lanka's foreign ownership rules allow foreign nationals to own condominium units only above the 4th floor, a restriction intended to prevent foreign ownership of entire buildings while allowing some investment in high-rise developments.

laws.title: Sri Lanka Consumer Affairs Authority
laws.subtitle: Price control and consumer rights enforcement
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka's Consumer Affairs Authority Act (No. 9/2003) established the CAA to regulate prices of essential goods, investigate unfair trade practices, and protect consumer rights. During Sri Lanka's 2022 economic crisis — the worst since independence — the CAA faced enormous pressure to control prices of fuel, medicine, and food amid severe shortages and hyperinflation. The National Price Commission can set maximum prices for essential goods. The Trade Measurement Act governs weights and measures. Consumer protection in financial services falls under the Central Bank's Financial Consumer Protection Unit. The 2022 crisis highlighted the challenges of consumer protection during a full economic collapse.
laws.penalty: CAA violation: fine up to LKR 1 million and product seizure; price control violation: criminal prosecution
exceptions: 2022 economic crisis tested Sri Lanka's consumer protection system severely
CAA has authority to set maximum prices for essential goods
laws.sourceLabel: Sri Lanka Consumer Affairs Authority Act

quiz.q: What unprecedented consumer protection challenge did Sri Lanka face in 2022?
options: Severe economic collapse causing hyperinflation, shortages, and complete supply chain breakdown
A cybercrime wave targeting online shoppers
quiz.explanation: Sri Lanka's 2022 economic crisis — its worst since independence — created extreme consumer protection challenges: fuel and medicine shortages, foreign exchange collapse, 50%+ food price inflation, and supply chain breakdown made normal consumer rights enforcement largely meaningless amid basic goods unavailability.

laws.title: Constitution of Sri Lanka, 1978
laws.subtitle: Executive presidency and Sinhala Buddhist nationalism in Sri Lanka's constitutional framework
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka's 1978 Constitution created a powerful executive presidency (later reformed by 19th and 22nd Amendments). The Sinhalese majority (74%) being predominantly Buddhist shapes politics: Buddhism has a 'foremost place' under Article 9 — unique in a democratic constitution. The Tamil minority (15%) has faced systemic discrimination: the 1956 Official Language Act making Sinhala the sole official language ('Sinhala Only' Act) ignited ethnic tensions that eventually became a 26-year civil war (1983-2009) between government forces and the LTTE (Tamil Tigers). The war ended with government victory but accusations of war crimes (40,000+ Tamil civilian deaths in final offensive). Post-war reconciliation remains incomplete.
laws.penalty: Constitutional rights violations: fundamental rights petitions to Supreme Court within one month. Emergency Regulations (Article 155) allow suspension of rights.
exceptions: Tamil has co-official status in Northern and Eastern Provinces
Tamils in Indian-origin plantations (Indian Tamils) have specific citizenship protections
Muslims (8% of population) have their own personal law (Muslim Marriage and Divorce Act)

quiz.q: What provision makes Sri Lanka's constitution unusual among democratic countries?
options: The constitution designates the military as an equal branch of government
Buddhism has a 'foremost place' under Article 9 — unique in giving a religion privileged constitutional status in a democracy
Sri Lanka's constitution prohibits political parties from forming coalitions
The President cannot be impeached under any circumstances
quiz.explanation: Article 9 of Sri Lanka's constitution mandates that the state shall 'protect and foster' Buddhism, which 'occupies the foremost place among religions'. This formal constitutional privileging of a religion is unusual in democracies — most democratic constitutions either establish religious neutrality or allow religious freedom equally. Combined with Buddhist nationalism in politics, Article 9 has been used to justify discrimination against Tamil Hindus, Muslims, and Christians, and has influenced laws and policies on religious conversion.

laws.title: Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) — Sri Lanka
laws.subtitle: Draconian security law used against civil society
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka's Prevention of Terrorism Act (1979) allows detention without charge for up to 18 months and confessions obtained in custody are admissible as evidence — despite documented torture. Originally designed for LTTE counter-terrorism, the PTA has been used extensively against Tamil civilians, journalists, civil society activists, and after the 2019 Easter Sunday bombings, against Muslims. Sri Lanka came under international pressure to repeal or reform the PTA, including from the EU (which threatened GSP+ trade preferences). Partial reforms were enacted but human rights organizations say the revised law retains core abusive elements. Sri Lanka withdrew from UN Human Rights Council co-sponsorship of resolution establishing transitional justice mechanism under Gotabaya Rajapaksa.
laws.penalty: Detention without charge: up to 18 months. Confessions obtained during detention admissible even without lawyer present. Terrorism: life imprisonment. Broad definition of terrorism includes non-violent acts.
exceptions: Recent PTA amendments nominally require judicial oversight at earlier stages
International organizations and diplomats may request access to detained foreign nationals
Bail applications may be made after 3 months of detention (previously 18 months)

quiz.q: What makes confessions under Sri Lanka's PTA particularly problematic?
options: Confessions must be in Sinhala even for Tamil suspects
PTA confessions obtained during detention are admissible without lawyer present — despite documented torture — creating incentive for coerced confessions
Suspects must confess before any charge can be filed
All PTA confessions are automatically presented to the UN Human Rights Council
quiz.explanation: Sri Lanka's PTA allows confessions obtained during detention to be used as evidence — even when the suspect had no access to a lawyer. This creates a perverse incentive for authorities: detaining someone and coercing a confession is an 'efficient' path to conviction. Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, and UN bodies have documented torture of PTA detainees and criticize the admissibility of confessions as enabling systematic abuse. The legal rule essentially rewards tortured confessions.

laws.title: IMF Bailout 2022-23 — Sri Lanka's Economic Collapse
laws.subtitle: Sri Lanka's unprecedented sovereign default and economic crisis
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka experienced an unprecedented economic crisis in 2022: the first time since independence (1948) that Sri Lanka defaulted on its foreign debt. Causes: excessive borrowing for vanity infrastructure projects (Hambantota Port, Mattala Airport — 'Ghost Airport'), tax cuts by Gotabaya Rajapaksa reducing revenue, COVID-19 destroying tourism (15% of GDP), a reckless overnight ban on chemical fertilizers (destroying agriculture), and the Ukraine war increasing import costs. By mid-2022: 13-hour daily power cuts, fuel queues of miles, medicine and food shortages. Massive protests stormed the Presidential Palace; President Gotabaya fled to Maldives then Singapore. Sri Lanka secured a $2.9B IMF program (2023) and restructured debt.
laws.penalty: Central bank violations: administrative and criminal sanctions under Monetary Law Act. Forex violations: up to 5 years imprisonment. Bank insolvency: CBSL-managed resolution.
exceptions: IMF program conditions create 'prior actions' superseding normal budgetary processes
Revenue measures mandated by IMF may override domestic political opposition
State enterprise reforms required by IMF may override sectoral legislation

quiz.q: What caused Sri Lanka's unprecedented economic collapse and sovereign default in 2022?
options: A natural disaster destroying 90% of the country's infrastructure
Multiple factors: excessive borrowing, tax cuts, COVID crushing tourism, a disastrous fertilizer ban, and Ukraine war import costs — combined in a perfect storm
A US trade embargo imposed after a human rights dispute
Sri Lanka was economically sabotaged by India in retaliation for Hambantota Port Chinese investment
quiz.explanation: Sri Lanka's 2022 collapse was caused by converging factors: decades of borrowing (Hambantota Port and other projects financed by Chinese loans), Gotabaya Rajapaksa's 2019 tax cuts reducing revenue by 2% of GDP, COVID-19 destroying tourism (15% of GDP), an overnight fertilizer ban causing the rice harvest to collapse by 50%, and the 2022 Ukraine war increasing food and fuel import costs. The forex reserves drained to near-zero — unable to import basics. The result: a country that had never defaulted in 74 years of independence did so in 2022.

laws.title: National Environmental Act — Sri Lanka
laws.subtitle: Environmental law in a biodiversity hotspot
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka's National Environmental Act (1980, amended) governs environmental protection in one of the world's biodiversity hotspots: Sri Lanka has 3,200+ flowering plant species (25% endemic), 435+ bird species, and the world's highest density of endangered species per square kilometer. The Central Environmental Authority (CEA) enforces environmental standards. Despite this biodiversity, Sri Lanka faces significant threats: coral bleaching, plastic pollution, sand mining from rivers and beaches destroying ecosystems, and agricultural chemical runoff. The 2022 fertilizer ban was intended to shift to organic agriculture but was implemented without planning, consultation, or transition support — causing catastrophic food production decline.
laws.penalty: Environmental Impact Assessment violations: project suspension and fines. Industrial pollution: administrative fines and environmental court proceedings. Sand mining without permit: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Small-scale artisanal fishing in coastal areas has modified marine conservation requirements
Traditional sustainable forestry practices in community forest areas
Emergency water supply projects may have expedited EIA processes

quiz.q: What makes Sri Lanka notable in terms of global biodiversity?
options: Sri Lanka is completely deforested — only mangroves survive
Sri Lanka has the world's highest density of endangered species per square kilometer — a biodiversity hotspot
Sri Lanka hosts the world's largest concentration of wild elephants
Sri Lanka has more endemic plant species than all of Africa combined
quiz.explanation: Sri Lanka is a globally recognized biodiversity hotspot: the island has 3,200+ plant species (25% found nowhere else), 435+ bird species (33% endemic), 100+ reptile species (50%+ endemic), and the world's highest density of endangered species relative to land area. This extraordinary biodiversity in a relatively small country (65,000 km²) results from Sri Lanka's geological history (ancient Gondwana land fragment), diverse habitats (tropical rainforest to dry zone to cloud forest), and geographic isolation.

laws.title: War Crimes Accountability — End of Civil War
laws.subtitle: Sri Lanka's unresolved accountability for 2009 war crimes
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka's 26-year civil war (1983-2009) between the government and LTTE (Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam) ended with a government offensive that killed 40,000+ Tamil civilians in the final months according to UN estimates. The war crimes included: deliberate shelling of hospitals and No Fire Zones, denial of food and medicine to civilians, summary executions of LTTE surrendering forces (White Flag case), and enforced disappearances. Sri Lanka established an Office on Missing Persons and Office for Reparations, but comprehensive accountability mechanism has not been implemented. Sri Lanka withdrew from co-sponsorship of a UN Human Rights Council resolution creating a hybrid justice mechanism under Rajapaksa government.
laws.penalty: War crimes under Sri Lanka's own laws: Penal Code murder and grievous hurt provisions (limited). International accountability: UN mechanisms and universal jurisdiction (limited).
exceptions: Combatants on both sides had individual legal obligations under laws of war
Humanitarian workers (ICRC, UN) had modified access agreements
Tamil diaspora funding of LTTE classified as terrorist financing under foreign laws

quiz.q: What is the UN's estimate of Tamil civilian deaths in the final months of Sri Lanka's civil war?
options: About 3,000 — comparable to other counterinsurgency operations
An estimated 40,000+ civilians killed in the final offensive — creating a major accountability gap
The UN found no evidence of civilian deaths — only combatant casualties
quiz.explanation: UN investigations and expert panels estimated 40,000-70,000 Tamil civilians were killed in the final months of Sri Lanka's civil war (2009), when the government offensive trapped civilians in shrinking zones. Evidence documented deliberate shelling of hospitals, No Fire Zones designated for civilians, and extrajudicial killings. Sri Lanka has never held comprehensive accountability for these killings, and the UN Human Rights Council has repeatedly passed resolutions on Sri Lanka, though implementation has been blocked by Sri Lanka's allies (China, India, Russia).

laws.title: Board of Investment Sri Lanka & Tourism Law
laws.subtitle: Sri Lanka's tourism recovery and investment framework
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka's Board of Investment (BOI) and tourism sector are central to economic recovery. Tourism was 15% of GDP before COVID-19; in 2019, 2.3 million tourists generated $3.6B. The Easter Sunday attacks (April 2019, 269 killed including 45 foreigners in hotels and churches by Islamist attackers) devastated tourism before COVID completed the destruction. Recovery has been slow: 1M tourists in 2022, 1.5M in 2023. Sri Lanka had natural tourism advantages: wildlife (leopards, elephants, blue whales), beaches, ancient ruins (Sigiriya, Anuradhapura), and tea estates. The 2022 economic crisis created additional deterrence. Sri Lanka is implementing debt restructuring and IMF structural reforms to restore investor confidence.
laws.penalty: BOI license violations: penalties and license revocation. Tourism business without license: administrative fines. Tourist area environmental violations: Environmental Court proceedings.
exceptions: Humanitarian missions may enter without tourism license
Diplomatic missions have modified visa requirements
Academic researchers may enter restricted areas with research permits

quiz.q: What 2019 attack severely damaged Sri Lanka's tourism industry before COVID made it worse?
options: A LTTE revival attack targeting foreign tourists in Colombo
The Easter Sunday bombings by Islamic State-linked militants killing 269 people including 45 foreigners in hotels and churches
A ferry accident killing cruise passengers near Galle
A tsunami warning causing mass tourist evacuations that never returned
quiz.explanation: The Easter Sunday attacks on April 21, 2019, saw coordinated bombings of three churches and three luxury hotels in Colombo and Negombo, killing 269 people (including 45 foreigners) on Easter morning when hotels and churches were full. Islamic State-linked Jamaat ul Mujahideen Sri Lanka carried out the attacks. Tourist arrivals immediately collapsed. Before any recovery, COVID-19 hit in 2020. Combined with the 2022 economic collapse, Sri Lanka's tourism sector suffered an unprecedented multi-year crisis despite the country's natural appeal.

laws.title: Immigrants and Emigrants Act — Sri Lanka
laws.subtitle: Overseas migration and diaspora remittances
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka has a significant migration pattern: 2.1+ million Sri Lankans work overseas, primarily in the Middle East (Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, Qatar) doing domestic work and construction. Remittances are a major foreign exchange source: $5-6B annually (8-10% of GDP). Sri Lanka's economy is so dependent on remittances that economic crisis management includes incentivizing overseas workers to channel remittances through formal banking rather than informal hawala. Female domestic workers in the Middle East face exploitation, abuse, and in some cases death — Sri Lanka has temporarily banned female domestic worker migration to certain countries (Saudi Arabia at various times) due to abuse concerns. The diaspora (primarily UK, Canada, Australia) provides different skills and capital.
laws.penalty: Human trafficking of migrants: up to 20 years imprisonment. Illegal money transfer channels: administrative fines. Operating unlicensed foreign employment agency: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Overseas Sri Lankans may invest in foreign currency bonds (Sri Lanka Development Bonds) under special investment schemes
Diaspora remittances through banking channels receive no Sri Lankan tax
Highly skilled diaspora returnees under incentive programs receive modified entry conditions
laws.sourceLabel: Sri Lanka Bureau of Foreign Employment

quiz.q: What protection concern has led Sri Lanka to periodically ban female domestic worker migration to certain Middle Eastern countries?
options: Sri Lanka banned migration to protect domestic labor supply for garment factories
Female domestic workers suffered exploitation, physical abuse, and death at the hands of employers — prompting temporary bans to specific countries
Sri Lanka banned migration to enforce remittance repatriation requirements
Female domestic workers were returning with 'foreign ideas' incompatible with Sri Lankan culture
quiz.explanation: Sri Lankan female domestic workers in the Middle East (Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, UAE) have faced severe exploitation: employers confiscating passports, non-payment of wages, physical and sexual abuse, and in documented cases, murder. Sri Lanka has periodically banned domestic worker migration to Saudi Arabia and Kuwait after particularly egregious cases drew media attention. However, the bans are often reversed due to remittance dependency, creating a cycle of short-term protection and return to risky migration.

laws.title: Online Safety Act 2024 & Digital Rights in Sri Lanka
laws.subtitle: New digital law threatening freedom of expression
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka's Online Safety Act (2024) established the Online Safety Commission with power to designate 'prohibited statements' and compel platforms to remove content. The Act was passed amid concern from digital rights organizations that its broad powers to define prohibited online speech (including 'false statements that are likely to cause public disorder') would be used to silence dissent. Sri Lanka has a history of using Information and Communication Technology Act Section 65B to prosecute critics. In post-economic-crisis Sri Lanka, political satire, criticism of government policies, and protest coordination increasingly occur online — making digital speech laws particularly consequential.
laws.penalty: Making prohibited statements online: up to 5 years imprisonment. Failing to comply with Online Safety Commission orders: up to 1 year for platforms. Impersonation online: up to 3 years.
exceptions: Educational and research content explicitly excluded if clearly labeled
Satire and commentary on public figures nominally protected under artistic expression
Foreign media organizations' content hosted abroad may be blocked rather than prosecuted

quiz.q: What concern did digital rights organizations raise about Sri Lanka's Online Safety Act?
options: The Act would require all online purchases to go through government-monitored payment systems
Broad powers to define 'prohibited statements' could be used to silence dissent — similar to other Asian digital censorship laws
The Act required all Sri Lankan citizens to use government-provided internet service
Online gambling and adult content were explicitly legalized, contradicting existing laws
quiz.explanation: Digital rights organizations (Access Now, EFF, local organizations) raised concerns that the Online Safety Commission's power to designate 'prohibited statements' — including content causing 'public disorder' — was vague enough to criminalize legitimate dissent, political satire, and criticism of government. The concern reflects patterns seen elsewhere in Asia (India's IT Act, Pakistan's PECA, Bangladesh's DSA) where cyber laws designed for genuine harm prevention are deployed against journalists, activists, and political opponents.

laws.title: Termination of Employment Act & Sri Lankan Labor Law
laws.subtitle: Worker protections and labor disputes in Sri Lanka
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka's labor laws include the Termination of Employment of Workmen Act (TEWA, 1971), Employees' Provident Fund Act, and Wages Boards Ordinance. TEWA makes dismissal of workers with 1+ year tenure extremely difficult: requires Ministry of Labour approval for any dismissal for non-misconduct reasons. Compensation for approved dismissals is high (up to 2.5 months per year of service). This system, designed to protect workers, was criticized as making Sri Lanka's labor market inflexible and discouraging formal employment. Sri Lanka's garment sector (apparel exports $5B) relies on female workers. EPZ workers have modified labor rights. The Free Trade Zone has seen major strikes, with security forces used against striking workers.
laws.penalty: Wrongful dismissal under TEWA: reinstatement or up to 2.5 months' pay per year of service. Labor standards violations: administrative fines and Wages Boards enforcement.
exceptions: Domestic workers not covered by most labor laws
Workers in export processing zones have modified industrial relations framework
Casual workers (non-permanent, under 1 year) not covered by TEWA

quiz.q: What makes Sri Lanka's Termination of Employment Act (TEWA) unusual from an employer perspective?
options: Employers may dismiss workers for any reason with 1-week notice
Dismissal of workers with 1+ year tenure for non-misconduct reasons requires Ministry of Labour approval — making firing very difficult
Workers can only be dismissed by a court order
TEWA requires employers to provide 3 years' severance for any dismissal
quiz.explanation: Sri Lanka's TEWA requires Ministry of Labour approval before dismissing a permanent employee for business reasons (redundancy, restructuring) — not just misconduct. Employers must file applications, demonstrate genuine business need, and pay compensation calculated by service years. This has been criticized as making Sri Lanka's labor market inflexible (employers hesitate to hire permanently if they cannot downsize later) and contributing to high informal employment. The World Bank has repeatedly cited TEWA in assessments of Sri Lanka's business environment.

laws.title: Sri Lanka National Health Policy — Free Universal Healthcare
laws.subtitle: Sri Lanka's free universal health system — a model for developing nations
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka provides free universal healthcare: all government hospitals provide free services to citizens — outpatient, inpatient, surgery, specialist care, and medicines. Sri Lanka achieves outcomes comparable to middle-income countries: life expectancy 77 years, maternal mortality 36/100,000, infant mortality 8/1,000 — remarkable for a lower-middle income country. This 'Sri Lanka model' is studied globally. The system faces challenges: doctor and nurse emigration to better-paying countries ('brain drain'), the 2022 economic crisis causing medicine shortages (pharmaceutical imports fell 40%), and facility maintenance. Sri Lanka also has a significant private hospital sector serving middle class and medical tourists (particularly cataract surgery and orthopedics).
laws.penalty: Operating unlicensed medical facility: criminal prosecution. Practicing medicine without license: up to 2 years imprisonment. Medicine fraud: up to 5 years.
exceptions: Ayurvedic and traditional medicine practitioners licensed under separate Ayurveda Act
Rural community health workers may provide basic care without full medical license
Emergency care must be provided by all hospitals regardless of patient's ability to pay or insurance status

quiz.q: What makes Sri Lanka's healthcare system remarkable for its income level?
options: Sri Lanka has the highest healthcare spending in South Asia
Free universal care at government hospitals achieves life expectancy of 77 years and very low maternal mortality — comparable to much richer nations
Sri Lanka attracted so many medical tourists it built the region's largest hospital
Sri Lanka has a higher doctor-to-patient ratio than the United States
quiz.explanation: Sri Lanka's free universal government healthcare system achieves outcomes comparable to high-middle income countries (life expectancy 77, maternal mortality 36/100,000, infant mortality 8/1,000) at lower-middle income country spending levels. The 'Sri Lanka model' — combining free government healthcare with a private sector safety valve — is cited by development economists as evidence that good health outcomes don't require high income. The 2022 economic crisis, which caused medicine shortages, starkly illustrated how fragile this achievement can be.

laws.title: Anti-Corruption Laws — Sri Lanka Bribery Commission
laws.subtitle: Corruption challenges and anti-corruption enforcement
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka's Bribery Act and Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery and Corruption (CIABOC) address corruption, which has been a significant governance challenge. Sri Lanka's 2022 economic crisis was partly attributed to governance failures and corrupt infrastructure projects. The Rajapaksa family dominated Sri Lankan politics for decades: brothers Mahinda (President), Gotabaya (also President), Basil (Finance Minister), Chamal (Speaker) — all serving simultaneously at one point. The family is linked to allegations of corrupt contracts, bond scams, and patronage. The 2015-2019 Sirisena-Wickremesinghe government's investigation of the Central Bank bond scandal was a landmark anti-corruption effort.
laws.penalty: Bribery of government official: up to 7 years imprisonment. Corruption involving public property: up to 7 years. Bribery of magistrate/judge: up to 10 years. Asset forfeiture available for all corruption offenses.
exceptions: Whistleblowers who cooperate with CIABOC may receive reduced prosecution exposure
Public officers making good-faith decisions later found erroneous are protected from corruption prosecution
Administrative settlements may be reached for minor regulatory corruption
laws.sourceLabel: Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery and Corruption Sri Lanka

quiz.q: What governance problem symbolized Sri Lanka's corruption challenges under the Rajapaksa family?
options: Sri Lanka's judges were found to be completely independent of political influence
Multiple family members held top government positions simultaneously — President, Finance Minister, Speaker — creating a family political monopoly linked to corrupt contracts
The Rajapaksa family donated their personal fortunes to reduce Sri Lanka's national debt
A whistleblower in the Rajapaksa government exposed corruption, leading to landmark prosecutions
quiz.explanation: The Rajapaksa family's simultaneous hold on Sri Lanka's key government positions is extraordinary: Mahinda Rajapaksa (President 2005-2015, Prime Minister 2019-2022), Gotabaya Rajapaksa (President 2019-2022), Basil Rajapaksa (Finance Minister), Chamal Rajapaksa (Speaker, Minister) — all serving at the same time. This concentration of family power in a democracy facilitated governance without checks. Projects like Hambantota Port in Mahinda's home district with borrowed Chinese money, Mattala Airport (consistently the world's emptiest airport), and the Lotus Tower were linked to patronage.

laws.title: Tea Industry Act — Sri Lanka Ceylon Tea
laws.subtitle: Sri Lanka's iconic tea industry: heritage and challenges
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka is the world's 4th largest tea producer and a leading exporter of premium 'Ceylon Tea'. The tea industry — introduced by British planters after coffee blight destroyed plantations in the 1860s — shaped Sri Lanka's landscape and demography: Indian Tamil laborers (Malaiyaha Tamils) brought for tea estates form a distinct ethnic community (4% of population) with their own political parties. Ceylon Tea is a Geographical Indication (GI) protected mark. The Tea Board of Sri Lanka certifies authentic Ceylon Tea. Sri Lanka's 2022 fertilizer ban devastated tea production: the overnight ban on synthetic fertilizers reduced tea yields by 40% and some plantations used organic certification loss to bargain down worker wages — a crisis within a crisis.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent use of Ceylon Tea GI mark: civil and criminal IP infringement. Tea export without Board certification: customs and trade penalties. Food safety violations in tea processing: administrative sanctions.
exceptions: Estate workers have special labor protections under Wages Boards for Plantation Workers separate from general labor law
Regional Plantation Companies (privatized in 1990s) operate under TRSL/KEL framework with modified corporate structure
Organic tea certification through recognized international agencies exempt from Board's standard certification

quiz.q: How did the 2022 fertilizer ban affect Sri Lanka's tea industry?
options: Tea production increased because organic farming improved quality
The overnight ban on synthetic fertilizers reduced tea yields by 40% — a major blow to Sri Lanka's largest export commodity during the economic crisis
Tea was unaffected because it grows naturally without fertilizer
Sri Lanka's tea industry was replaced by coffee after the fertilizer ban
quiz.explanation: When President Gotabaya Rajapaksa banned all synthetic fertilizers overnight in April 2021 (with 6 months before reversal), tea farmers suffered immediately: tea plants need regular fertilization for production, and organic alternatives were unavailable at scale without transition time. Tea yields dropped 40%, affecting export earnings during a forex crisis when Sri Lanka desperately needed tea export revenue. The fertilizer ban — intended to save forex on fertilizer imports and promote organic farming — instead accelerated the very forex crisis it was meant to help.

laws.title: Equal Opportunity Laws and Minority Rights in Sri Lanka
laws.subtitle: Constitutional rights and ethnic discrimination in Sri Lanka
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka's constitution guarantees equality but ethnic discrimination against Tamils has been systemic. The Official Language Act 1956 (Sinhala Only) sparked Tamil protests and eventual civil war. Tamil-medium education was restricted, reducing Tamil access to government employment. The Standardization Policy (1971) required higher university entry marks for Tamil students — effectively reducing Tamil university admission proportionally, a form of ethnic affirmative action for the Sinhala majority. These policies drove Tamil grievances that fueled the LTTE insurgency. Post-war, language policy has evolved: Tamil is co-official, government departments are required to provide Tamil services in Northern and Eastern provinces.
laws.penalty: Ethnic discrimination in government employment: administrative remedies and civil rights petitions. Language rights violations by government: fundamental rights petition to Supreme Court.
exceptions: Affirmative action for marginalized communities (women, disabled) is constitutionally permitted
Religious and language communities may establish and administer their own educational institutions
Private employment decisions on linguistic ability may be justified by genuine job requirements
laws.sourceLabel: Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka

quiz.q: What education policy in Sri Lanka deliberately reduced Tamil university admission to give the Sinhala majority proportional representation?
options: Sri Lanka's Sinhala Only Act closed all Tamil-medium schools
The Standardization Policy (1971) required higher exam marks for Tamil students — effectively reducing Tamil university admission while increasing Sinhala representation
Sri Lanka banned Tamil language instruction at university level
Tamil students were required to pay higher tuition than Sinhala students
quiz.explanation: Sri Lanka's Standardization Policy (1971) was applied to university admissions: because Tamil students historically scored higher in competitive exams than Sinhala students (reflecting different educational traditions and language test advantages), 'standardized' admission required Tamil applicants to achieve higher marks for the same university places. The policy was framed as ensuring ethnic proportionality in universities, but Tamils experienced it as discrimination that blocked merit-based advancement. This policy is cited by Tamil nationalists as evidence of systematic discrimination that justified their separatist cause.

laws.title: Wildlife Conservation Ordinance — Elephant-Human Conflict
laws.subtitle: Sri Lanka's threatened elephants and human-wildlife conflict
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka has the world's highest density of Asian elephants (7,000+ elephants in 65,000 km², about 60-70 per 1,000 km²). The Wildlife Conservation Ordinance (1937, amended) protects elephants. Human-elephant conflict is severe: elephants killed 100+ people annually and humans kill 250-300 elephants annually (electric fencing, shooting, hakka patas — explosive food). Sri Lanka has tried electric fences, elephant drives, and translocation. The elephant's cultural significance is profound: the Temple of the Tooth Relic in Kandy holds major festivals (Esala Perahera) with 100+ elephants; elephant captivity is deeply integrated into religious and cultural life. Captive elephants are registered and regulated but often kept in poor conditions.
laws.penalty: Killing or injuring elephant: up to 3 years and Rs250,000 fine. Capturing elephant without permit: up to 3 years. Illegal wildlife trade including ivory: up to 5 years.
exceptions: Perahera elephants registered under the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance may participate in religious processions
Elephant sanctuaries (Pinnawala) operate under Wildlife Department oversight with modified feeding and veterinary requirements
Translocation of conflict elephants may be ordered by Wildlife Department
laws.sourceLabel: Department of Wildlife Conservation Sri Lanka

quiz.q: What makes Sri Lanka's human-elephant conflict particularly severe and difficult to resolve?
options: Sri Lanka has no elephants — the problem is with leopards, not elephants
Sri Lanka has the world's highest elephant density AND growing human population — both needing the same shrinking habitat, with 100+ people and 250-300 elephants killed annually
Sri Lanka's elephants are domesticated and the conflict is about ownership disputes
Sri Lanka imported 1,000 elephants from Africa which don't coexist peacefully with local wildlife
quiz.explanation: Sri Lanka's human-elephant conflict is structurally driven: 7,000 elephants in 65,000 km² coexist with 22 million people in an increasingly fragmented landscape. As agricultural land expands into traditional elephant habitat, elephants raid crops and people are killed in encounters; people kill elephants with electric fences, poison, and explosive-laden food (hakka patas). Both sides lose. Sri Lanka's government struggles to balance elephant conservation (culturally and ecologically vital), farmer livelihoods, and public safety in a country where every kilometer is inhabited.

laws.title: Inland Revenue Act Sri Lanka & Tax Revenue
laws.subtitle: Tax reform under IMF pressure in post-crisis Sri Lanka
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka's Inland Revenue Act (2017) consolidated income tax legislation. Tax revenue was severely reduced by Gotabaya Rajapaksa's 2019 tax cuts: VAT reduced from 15% to 8%, income tax thresholds raised, 7 minor taxes abolished. These cuts reduced revenue by 2% of GDP — a significant factor in the subsequent economic collapse. The IMF program (2023) required reversing these cuts: VAT back to 18%, income tax reform, corporate tax increases, elimination of exemptions. Sri Lanka's tax policy lesson — that populist tax cuts in a fragile economy can trigger sovereign default — has become a case study in development economics.
laws.penalty: Income tax evasion: up to 3 years imprisonment and triple the evaded amount. VAT fraud: up to 5 years and administrative penalties. Transfer pricing manipulation: administrative penalties and adjusted assessments.
exceptions: Export-oriented businesses receive income tax holidays on export earnings
Charitable organizations registered with Commissioner General of Inland Revenue exempt from income tax on donations
Employee provident fund contributions exempt from income tax

quiz.q: How did Sri Lanka's 2019 tax cuts contribute to its 2022 economic collapse?
options: The tax cuts attracted so much foreign investment it overheated the economy
Reducing VAT from 15% to 8% and raising income tax thresholds cut revenue by 2% of GDP — worsening the fiscal deficit that contributed to sovereign default
Tax cuts increased tax evasion through loopholes in the new legislation
The 2019 tax cuts were reversed immediately and had no economic effect
quiz.explanation: President Gotabaya Rajapaksa's 2019 tax cuts (reducing VAT from 15% to 8%, abolishing smaller taxes, raising income tax thresholds) were implemented just before COVID-19. The revenue reduction of approximately 2% of GDP came precisely when the economy needed resources for pandemic response. Combined with COVID destroying tourism revenue, fertilizer ban damaging agriculture, and Ukraine war increasing import costs, the fiscal gap became impossible to fill. Sri Lanka's experience is cited as a textbook case of how populist tax cuts in a vulnerable fiscal position can be macroeconomically catastrophic.

laws.title: Penal Code Sri Lanka — Section 365 and LGBTQ+ Criminalization
laws.subtitle: Sri Lanka's criminalization of same-sex relations
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka's Penal Code retains Section 365 criminalizing 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' — effectively criminalizing same-sex relations. This colonial-era provision (inherited from British Indian Penal Code) carries up to 10 years imprisonment. Sri Lanka has not decriminalized same-sex relations despite India doing so in 2018. Sri Lanka's LGBTQ+ community faces police harassment and arrests under Section 365. The government has repeatedly indicated it will not repeal the provision citing religious and cultural grounds. Sri Lanka's constitution does not include sexual orientation in its equality provisions. LGBTQ+ activists operate under significant constraints.
laws.penalty: Carnal intercourse against order of nature (Section 365): up to 10 years imprisonment. Sexual harassment: up to 5 years. Gross indecency between males (Section 365A): up to 2 years.
exceptions: Private consensual adult activity may be prosecuted under the law — no private sphere exemption
Foreign nationals are subject to the same law if conduct occurs in Sri Lanka
There is no anti-discrimination protection for LGBTQ+ individuals in employment or services

quiz.q: How does Sri Lanka's approach to same-sex relations compare to neighboring India's?
options: Sri Lanka legalized same-sex marriage in 2022, well ahead of India
India decriminalized same-sex relations in 2018 (Section 377 ruling), but Sri Lanka retains its criminalization provision (Section 365) despite regional legal evolution
Both countries criminalized same-sex relations in the same colonial-era legislation and neither has changed this
Sri Lanka has always been more progressive than India on LGBTQ+ rights
quiz.explanation: India's Supreme Court struck down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code in 2018 — decriminalizing same-sex relations for the first time since the colonial period. Sri Lanka retains its equivalent provision (Section 365) criminalizing 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' with up to 10 years imprisonment. The contrast is stark: neighboring Nepal's Supreme Court ordered same-sex marriage legalization in 2023; India decriminalized in 2018; but Sri Lanka has made no progress toward decriminalization, with the government citing religious sentiment.

laws.title: Indian Tamil Citizenship Issue — Estate Tamil Communities
laws.subtitle: Statelessness and citizenship of Indian Tamils in Sri Lanka
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka's Indian Tamil (Malaiyaha Tamil) community — descendants of laborers brought by British colonists for tea estates in the 19th-20th centuries — faced a statelessness crisis at independence. The Citizenship Act 1948 excluded most Indian Tamils from citizenship, rendering 1 million people stateless. The Sirima-Shastri Pact (1964) and subsequent agreements between Sri Lanka and India provided for 600,000 to become Indian citizens, 375,000 to become Sri Lankan citizens, and remaining numbers resolved later. The process took decades. Most estate Tamils now have Sri Lankan citizenship but remain economically marginalized: living in line rooms on tea estates with limited education access and minimal land ownership.
laws.penalty: Working in Sri Lanka without valid citizenship or residency: deportation risk (for those with residency documentation uncertainty). Employment of undocumented workers: administrative fines.
exceptions: India-Sri Lanka bilateral agreements govern remaining disputed citizenship cases
Estate Tamil workers on tea plantations have modified collective housing rights under plantation law
Plantation workers' children born in Sri Lanka have citizenship by birth under 2003 amendments
laws.sourceLabel: Department of Immigration and Emigration Sri Lanka

quiz.q: Why were Indian Tamils in Sri Lanka rendered stateless after independence?
options: Indian Tamils voluntarily gave up citizenship to maintain Indian passports for economic benefits
The 1948 Citizenship Act excluded Indian Tamils — making approximately 1 million people stateless — because they couldn't prove generations of Sri Lankan ancestry
Sri Lanka deported all Indian Tamils to India after independence
Indian Tamils were stateless because India refused to accept them as Indian citizens
quiz.explanation: When Ceylon became independent (1948), the Citizenship Act required applicants to prove that their grandparents were born in Ceylon — a requirement Indian Tamils brought to tea estates in the 19th-20th centuries could not meet. Approximately 1 million Indian Tamils became stateless overnight. Decades of bilateral negotiations (Sirima-Shastri Pact 1964, Sirima-Indira Gandhi Pact 1974) gradually resolved most cases, granting either Sri Lankan or Indian citizenship. The delay — some cases took until the 1980s-90s to resolve — left a community in legal limbo for 30-50 years.

laws.title: Emergency Regulations and State of Emergency — Sri Lanka
laws.subtitle: Sri Lanka's extensive use of emergency powers
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka's Public Security Ordinance (1947) and constitutional emergency provisions have been used extensively. The state of emergency was in force almost continuously from 1971-2011 — essentially normalizing emergency rule. Emergency regulations allowed: detention without trial, curfew enforcement, search without warrant, and military jurisdiction over civilians. During the civil war period, emergency rule was the permanent background to governance. Emergency was declared again in 2022 during the economic crisis and anti-Rajapaksa protests. Sri Lanka's extensive reliance on emergency powers has been criticized as creating a governance culture where normal rule-of-law safeguards are bypassed reflexively.
laws.penalty: Violation of emergency regulations (curfew, movement restrictions): administrative penalties and criminal prosecution. Obstruction of security forces under emergency: up to 3 years.
exceptions: Emergency regulations require periodic Parliamentary approval every month — providing nominal legislative oversight
Fundamental rights petitions may still be filed during emergency, though Supreme Court access is harder
Emergency does not suspend all rights — specific regulations must be passed for each restriction
laws.sourceLabel: Law Net — Ministry of Justice Sri Lanka

quiz.q: How long was Sri Lanka continuously under a declared state of emergency?
options: Sri Lanka has never declared a state of emergency in its entire history
Sri Lanka's state of emergency was in force almost continuously from 1971-2011 — essentially normalizing emergency governance for 40 years
Sri Lanka declared emergency only during the 2022 economic crisis
Sri Lanka has been under emergency since independence in 1948 without interruption
quiz.explanation: Sri Lanka was continuously or near-continuously under state of emergency from 1971 (when a JVP Marxist uprising was suppressed) through 2011 — a span of 40 years. Emergency regulations co-existed with democratic elections, but enabled detention without trial, military jurisdiction, and suspension of normal legal protections. Critics argue that normalizing emergency rule for 40 years created governance patterns where law enforcement instinctively uses extraordinary powers rather than normal legal process — a legacy affecting Sri Lanka's rule-of-law culture.

laws.title: Marine Resources Act — Fisheries and Coastal Management
laws.subtitle: Sri Lanka's fishing industry and maritime boundary disputes
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka's Marine Resources Act and Fisheries and Aquatic Resources Act govern the fishing industry. Sri Lanka has a 1,340 km coastline with extensive fishing communities. Sri Lankan fishermen in the Palk Strait (between Sri Lanka and India) have faced significant issues: Indian fishermen's use of bottom trawlers devastates marine ecosystems and competes with Sri Lankan artisanal fishers; Sri Lankan fishermen have been arrested by the Indian Coast Guard for crossing the maritime boundary; Tamil fishermen from northern Sri Lanka lost their boats and fishing access during the civil war. Sri Lanka has a significant aquaculture sector (shrimp and tilapia). The Exclusive Economic Zone (200 nautical miles) is administered under the Marine Resources Act.
laws.penalty: Fishing without license in Sri Lankan waters: confiscation of boat and gear plus fines. Use of prohibited fishing methods (dynamite, bottom trawling): criminal prosecution. Foreign vessel unauthorized fishing: detention and fine.
exceptions: Traditional fishing vessels below 25 feet operating within 3 nautical miles have simplified licensing
Artisanal fishers may sell fish directly without going through Fisheries Cooperative Society
Aquaculture operations above threshold require separate BOI-administered permits

quiz.q: What maritime boundary tension exists between Sri Lanka and India?
options: India claims the entire Palk Strait as Indian territorial waters
Indian fishermen's use of bottom trawlers in the Palk Strait damages marine ecosystems and the Sri Lankan government arrests Indian fishermen — causing diplomatic tensions between India and Sri Lanka
Sri Lanka and India dispute ownership of Adam's Bridge and the Gulf of Mannar
India and Sri Lanka have completely peaceful and uncontested maritime boundaries
quiz.explanation: The Palk Strait between Sri Lanka and India is a flashpoint: Indian fishermen (primarily from Tamil Nadu) use bottom-trawling nets that devastate marine ecosystems and compete directly with Sri Lankan artisanal fishers in northern Sri Lanka. Sri Lankan authorities arrest Indian fishermen who cross the maritime boundary. Tamil Nadu politicians in India are politically bound to defend Indian fishermen. Sri Lanka's Tamil fishermen, who are trying to rebuild after the civil war, face competition from better-equipped Indian trawlers. The dispute tests India-Sri Lanka relations regularly.

laws.title: Mental Health Act and Mental Health Services — Sri Lanka
laws.subtitle: Mental health law and services after civil war trauma
laws.fullDescription: Sri Lanka's Mental Health Act (1956, amended) governs mental health care. Sri Lanka faces significant mental health challenges: decades of civil war created trauma across the population; the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed 35,000 Sri Lankans and displaced 500,000; the 2022 economic crisis created acute economic anxiety and suicides. Sri Lanka has a relatively high suicide rate (17/100,000) — one of South Asia's highest. Mental health services remain concentrated in Colombo. Sri Lanka has pioneered community mental health initiatives in post-tsunami recovery. The Easter Sunday bombing survivors required specialized trauma support. Mental health awareness remains stigmatized in Sri Lankan society across ethnic communities.
laws.penalty: Involuntary commitment of person not meeting legal criteria: administrative review and habeas corpus remedy. Abuse of mental health patients: criminal prosecution. Operating unlicensed mental health facility: administrative closure.
exceptions: Traditional healing practitioners (Ayurveda, religious exorcism) are not prohibited but cannot claim to treat diagnosed psychiatric conditions
Community mental health workers may provide support and referral without clinical license
Emergency involuntary detention for 72 hours by police is permitted before judicial review

quiz.q: What combination of events has created significant mental health challenges in Sri Lanka?
options: Sri Lanka has no mental health challenges — it has universal mental health coverage
Civil war (26 years), 2004 tsunami (35,000 killed), 2022 economic collapse, and Easter Sunday bombings created compounding trauma and high suicide rates (17/100,000)
Only the 2022 economic crisis caused mental health issues; all other events are ancient history
Sri Lanka's mental health challenges are primarily genetic rather than event-driven
quiz.explanation: Sri Lanka has experienced extraordinary compounding trauma: 26 years of civil war affecting the entire population; the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killing 35,000 Sri Lankans and displacing 500,000; the 2019 Easter Sunday bombings (269 killed in coordinated attacks); and the 2022 economic crisis (with food/medicine shortages, power cuts, and economic despair). Sri Lanka's relatively high suicide rate (17/100,000) reflects these mental health pressures. The country has pioneered some community mental health responses (post-tsunami) but mental health services remain inadequate relative to population needs.
